title: Capstone: Designing a System End to End

questions.prompt: What should be the FIRST step when tackling a system design problem?

options.text: Draw the microservices architecture
Clarify the functional and non-functional requirements
Choose a database vendor
Set up Kafka

questions.explanation: Requirements (functional and non-functional) decide everything downstream. Jumping to architecture first risks solving the wrong problem or over-engineering.

questions.prompt: Why do estimation and requirements come before drawing the architecture?

options.text: They are just formalities
The requirements and scale numbers determine what architecture is actually needed
They slow you down on purpose
Architecture never depends on scale

questions.explanation: The scale estimates and requirements tell you whether you need one box or a fleet, and where caching, replicas, or partitioning are justified.

questions.prompt: In the URL shortener, why can redirects be served with eventual consistency?

options.text: Redirects must always be perfectly fresh
A newly created link appearing a moment late is acceptable, so favoring availability and low latency is a fine trade-off
Because URLs are encrypted
Eventual consistency is always required

questions.explanation: The read-heavy redirect path tolerates slight staleness, so an availability- and latency-favoring (AP-leaning) choice is appropriate. Only code uniqueness needs a strong guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which two questions most shape where you focus design effort?

options.text: The programming language and the cloud provider
The read:write ratio and the hot path
The team size and the deadline
The logo and the color scheme

questions.explanation: The read:write ratio and the hot path reveal whether to lean on caching/replicas (reads) or partitioning/queues (writes), and which operation must be fast.

questions.prompt: Why generate short codes with a counter + Base62 and per-server id ranges?

options.text: It encrypts the URLs
Base62-encoding a unique increasing id guarantees uniqueness with short codes, and per-server ranges avoid a single global-counter bottleneck
It makes redirects slower
It removes the need for a database

questions.explanation: Base62 of a unique id yields short, collision-free codes; handing each server a block of ids removes the hot single counter.

questions.prompt: How should you present a completed system design?

options.text: As the single correct answer with no alternatives
As a set of justified trade-offs with the current bottleneck named
As a list of technologies only
Without mentioning any weaknesses

questions.explanation: Strong designs are communicated as trade-offs (consistency vs latency, simplicity vs scale) with the bottleneck identified — there is rarely one 'right' answer.
